title: Ofe Oha
author: Jemimah Ogunleye
desc: Thickened with three or four cocoyams boiled in their skins and pounded smooth — and the oha leaves are shredded by hand, because cutting them with a knife is said to turn the soup bitter.
longDesc: Ofe oha is thickened with cocoyam rather than yam: three or four medium corms boiled in their skins with no salt for about twenty minutes, peeled, pounded or blended smooth, and then dropped into the soup in small dollops to dissolve over five or six minutes. The leaves are seasonal and they come with a rule — oha is torn by hand rather than cut with a knife, because knife-cutting is believed to make the soup bitter. Uziza goes in a minute before the oha, and the pot comes off the heat for the last two or three minutes.
ingredients: Assorted meats — beef, goat meat, ponmo, shaki
A handful of uziza leaves, or 1 tsp ground uziza seeds
steps: Soak the stockfish and smoked fish in hot water.
Boil the tough meats and the stockfish until soft.
Boil the cocoyams with their skins on, no salt, about 20 minutes until tender.
Peel them and pound or blend until smooth.
Add the smoked fish and the blended peppers to the meat pot and cook 5 minutes.
Add the palm oil and boil 6 to 8 minutes, until it is fully incorporated.
Add the cocoyam paste in small dollops and let it dissolve and combine over 5 to 6 minutes.
Add the ogiri igbo and cook 1 minute.
Add the uziza and cook 1 minute.
Shred the oha leaves by hand and add them. Take the pot off the heat and let it simmer 2 to 3 minutes on the residual heat.
chefTips: Tear the oha, do not cut it. Cutting with a knife is believed to make the soup bitter, and whatever the mechanism it is a rule people follow.
Cocoyam boils in its skin with no salt. Salt toughens it and peeling it first makes it waterlogged.
Small dollops, not one lump. Five or six minutes to dissolve is only achievable if the pieces are small.
Six to eight minutes on the palm oil before anything else, until it is fully incorporated. Raw palm oil in a finished soup tastes raw.
Uziza a minute before the oha. It is tougher and more peppery and needs the extra time.
Oha is seasonal. When it is out of season, bitter leaf or another green is the usual substitute but it is a different soup.
Achi or ofor can replace cocoyam as the thickener. Ofor belongs to this soup family — it is not used for nsala.
commonMistakes: Cutting the oha leaves with a knife.
Adding the cocoyam paste in one mass.
Boiling the soup after the oha goes in.
sources: Adapted from 'Ofe Oha (Oha/Ora Soup)', byline Sisi Jemimah. Quantities as printed: assorted meats (beef, goat meat, ponmo, shaki) — no quantity; 2 cooking spoons palm oil; 1 bunch oha leaves; handful uziza leaves or 1 teaspoon ground uziza seeds; 3–4 medium cocoyams (ede); smoked fish — no quantity; stockfish head (okporoko) — no quantity; 4 tablespoons ground crayfish; 1 tablespoon ogiri igbo; 2–3 yellow scotch bonnet; 2 maggi crayfish cubes; salt.

Her headnote notes the soup is 'popularly referred to as Ofe Oha by the Igbo people of Eastern Nigeria', that the leaves are seasonal, and — the cultural-technical point worth keeping — that oha is traditionally shredded BY HAND rather than cut with a knife, as cutting is believed to make the soup bitter.

Times and cues as printed: cocoyam boiled skins on, no salt, about 20 minutes until tender, then pounded or blended smooth; smoked fish plus peppers 5 minutes; palm oil boiled 6 to 8 minutes 'until fully incorporated'; cocoyam added in small dollops to dissolve and combine over 5 to 6 minutes; ogiri igbo 1 minute; uziza 1 minute; oha with the heat off, residual simmer 2 to 3 minutes. Yield not specified.

ON THE THICKENER: cocoyam, 3 to 4 medium, with ACHI OR OFOR named as the alternatives. This is one of only two places in any source consulted where ofor appears, and both are cocoyam soups rather than nsala — the other being 1Q Food Platter's ofe onugbu (NGA051). Ofor belongs to the oha and onugbu family.
NOTE: the assorted meats, the smoked fish and the stockfish head all carry no quantities on the page.

ON OHA, from 'African Vegetables (Leafy Greens)', byline Tayo Oredola, Low Carb Africa: oha or ora is Pterocarpus mildbraedii, 'Oha leaf/Ora leaf (Igbo)', from an evergreen tree 'cultivated in the eastern parts of Nigeria', used for 'the famous Oha soup, a rich, traditional soup loaded with ponmo (cow skin) and smoked fish'.

ON OGIRI IGBO specifically, and this matters because the condiment names are routinely confused: Kitchen Butterfly's article on fermented seeds identifies ogiri-igbo as being produced from castor oil seed, Ricinus communis — distinct from the ogiri she defines as fermented melon seed. See NGA120 for the full condiment tangle.
reheating: Low heat with a splash of water. The cocoyam thickening tightens cold.
healthBenefits: Cocoyam is a low-allergen starch rich in potassium and resistant starch.
Oha leaf supplies iron, calcium and vitamin A.
Very low in carbohydrate for a thickened soup.
culturalNote: Ofe oha is one of the soups by which an Igbo cook is judged, and its seasonality is part of its standing — oha leaves are not available all year, so the soup carries a sense of occasion that a year-round green could not. The hand-shredding rule is the kind of instruction that survives precisely because it is easy to transmit and costs nothing to follow.
